job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

response.passage: In our economics class today, we simulated how a multinational company (MNC) operates. We imagined a firm based in India that sets up manufacturing units in Vietnam and Brazil to reduce costs and access local markets. This proved that MNCs do not just produce goods in their home country, but strategically spread operations globally. We then discussed the role of the Indian government in the 1991 reforms. By removing trade barriers, the government actively shaped the economy, proving that globalisation is not an uncontrollable natural force but a policy-driven process. We also examined the World Trade Organization (WTO). While it sets rules for international trade, we discovered that developed nations often exert more influence than developing ones, meaning it is not a perfectly democratic body where everyone holds equal power. Finally, we looked at local toy makers. When trade barriers were removed, these small producers faced intense competition from cheaper imported goods, showing that liberalisation does not automatically benefit every local business. This activity highlighted that while globalisation integrates markets, its outcomes depend heavily on government regulations and the power dynamics between nations.
response.summary: This classroom activity explored how MNCs operate globally and how government policies shape the effects of globalisation. It also highlighted the power imbalances within international trade organizations and the mixed impact of liberalisation on local producers.
